note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Primary complaint: 3 days of watery → very loose diarrhea and persistent vomiting.
  - Possible exposure: contact with brother who has similar symptoms; patient reports "everyone in school's got this" per brother (possible infectious exposure).
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset: began 3 days ago.
  - Progression: started watery, now very loose stools; vomiting everything taken (including fluids) since this morning; feeling feverish for past few days.
  - Frequency: lost count of bowel motions; at least four episodes today. Last vomiting episode approximately 2 hours prior to call.
- ENT symptoms (as applicable):
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: not reported.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: not reported.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia: not reported.
  - Drooling: not reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: not reported.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: not reported.
  - Dyspnea: not reported.
  - Distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): not reported.
  - Ear/neck symptoms: not reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - No prior episodes of diarrhoea or constipation reported; bowel habits normally once daily.
  - No prior abdominal surgeries or chronic abdominal problems stated.
  - No prior hospitalizations or emergency injections mentioned.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: not stated.
  - Regular medications: vitamin D daily.
  - Other medications: oral rehydration salts (ORS) mix taken approximately three times daily for past two days; occasional ibuprofen for menstrual cramps (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Any relevant social context:
  - Lives with brother and mother.
  - Patient was in a private place for the consultation; working from home today (graphics designer).
  - Patient instructed to contact support line for appointment; doctor also stated they would arrange urgent appointment (conflict noted—see Quality checks).

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: not recorded / none stated.
- Airway/breathing descriptors: not recorded / none stated.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Patient coherent; reports feeling "literally boiling" (subjective fever); vomiting and abdominal pain.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Hydration indicators recorded verbally:
  - Patient reports passing urine about one hour prior to call.
  - No urine color reported.
- Presence of another person with the patient during consult: Not recorded (patient reported household members but was in a private place).

Assessment:
- Clinical impression:
  - Suspected infectious gastroenteritis, most likely viral given household contact (brother) with similar symptoms; bacterial cause not excluded.
  - Concern for dehydration due to persistent vomiting and inability to retain fluids.
- Key justifications from transcript:
  - Onset 3 days ago with watery diarrhea progressing to frequent very loose stools and persistent vomiting.
  - Household contact (brother) with similar symptoms suggesting infectious transmission.
  - Patient unable to keep down fluids, though did pass urine about one hour prior to call (indicates some ongoing urine output).
- Conflict noted:
  - Doctor advised the patient to book an appointment through the support line but also stated "we'll do that for you"—responsibility for arranging urgent clinic appointment is unclear.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Continue oral rehydration salts (ORS) in very small, frequent sips to minimize vomiting.
  - Advise simple bland foods if tolerated (toast or biscuit); avoid fruit, vegetables, and milk as they may worsen symptoms.
  - Arrange urgent clinic appointment for stool sample collection and formal hydration assessment (patient instructed to book via support line; doctor also indicated they would arrange booking — conflict noted).
  - If symptoms worsen, patient to be seen urgently in A&E.
- Specific instructions provided to patient/caregiver (verbatim where stated in transcript):
  - "If, in the meantime, you're feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in A and E."
  - "So you can call us back in the meantime."
  - "You'll have to book an appointment through the support line."
- Escalation criteria / red flags mentioned:
  - Any clinical deterioration or feeling "more unwell" → attend A&E.
  - Concern for progressive dehydration (inability to keep fluids down) prompting urgent assessment.
- Follow-up:
  - Urgent clinic visit planned for stool specimen submission and hydration check; appointment to be arranged via support line / by service (conflict noted).
  - Patient advised to call back if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.
- Other:
  - No discussion of ENT/allergy referral, epinephrine, or auto-injector (not applicable / not discussed).
  - No COVID-19 vaccine suitability discussion recorded.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Recorded vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate) — not recorded.
  - Physical examination findings (abdominal exam, signs of dehydration) — not recorded.
  - Exact stool frequency and stool characteristics beyond "very loose" — incomplete.
  - Urine color and volume details — not recorded beyond "passed urine an hour ago."
  - Allergies explicitly documented — not stated.
  - Pregnancy status or last menstrual details relative to potential acute care considerations — last period stated as two weeks ago; no pregnancy test discussed.
  - Stool sample status (collected vs pending) — pending; plan to obtain at clinic.
  - Medication doses/routes/frequencies for ibuprofen and vitamin D — not documented.
  - Clear documentation of who will book the urgent clinic appointment (patient via support line vs clinician arranging) — conflict noted.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - Responsibility for booking the urgent appointment: doctor told patient "you'll have to book an appointment through the support line" and later said "we'll do that for you."
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Audio/transcript generally clear with brief pauses and some short hesitations; clinically relevant details were audible and extractable.
